items.followUp: State the SI unit of kinetic energy and define it.

rubric.why: Identifies the SI unit of potential energy.
rubric.description: Names the joule as the SI unit.
rubric.how: Award for stating that potential energy is measured in joules (J).

rubric.why: Defines the joule in terms of work.
rubric.how: Award for stating that one joule is the work done by a force of one newton moving an object one metre in the force's direction.

modelAnswer: The SI unit of potential energy is the joule (J).
One joule is the work done when a force of 1 N moves an object through 1 m in the direction of the force.

items.followUp: Define compressive strain and write its formula.

rubric.why: Strain is the ratio of change in length to original length.
rubric.how: Award for giving the ratio of change in length to original (or initial) length.

rubric.why: Tensile strain is the extension per original length.
rubric.how: Award for stating the ratio of extension (increase in length) to original length.

modelAnswer: Strain is the ratio of the change in length of a body to its original length.
Tensile strain is the ratio of the increase in length (extension) to the original length.

items.followUp: A force of 40 N acts on an area of 2 m². Find the stress.

rubric.why: Stress is force per unit area.
rubric.description: Defines stress and gives its formula.
rubric.how: Award for stating stress is force per unit area and writing stress = force/area (or σ = F/A).

rubric.why: Stress is measured in pascals, equivalent to newtons per square metre.
rubric.how: Award for giving pascal (Pa) or N/m².

modelAnswer: Stress is the force acting per unit area of a body.
Stress = Force / Area, or σ = F/A.
The SI unit of stress is pascal (Pa), which is equal to N/m².

items.followUp: Using a speed-time graph, derive the relation v² = u² + 2as.

rubric.why: The area under the speed-time graph gives displacement.
rubric.how: Award for using the trapezium area to obtain S = ½(Vᵢ + Vf)t.

rubric.why: Uses the definition of acceleration.
rubric.how: Award for writing a = (Vf − Vᵢ)/t or its rearrangement.

rubric.why: Combines the displacement and acceleration expressions.
rubric.description: Eliminates time and forms the product.
rubric.how: Award for obtaining 2aS = (Vf − Vᵢ)(Vᵢ + Vf).

rubric.why: Completes the required identity by difference of squares.
rubric.how: Award for the final relation 2aS = Vf² − Vᵢ².

modelAnswer: For uniformly accelerated motion, the speed-time graph is a straight line from Vᵢ to Vf over time t.
The displacement S is the area of the trapezium under the graph: S = ½(Vᵢ + Vf)t.
Acceleration a = (Vf − Vᵢ)/t, so t = (Vf − Vᵢ)/a.
Substituting for t: 2aS = (Vᵢ + Vf)(Vf − Vᵢ) = Vf² − Vᵢ².

items.followUp: Derive the expression for the kinetic energy of a body of mass m moving with speed v.

rubric.why: Kinetic energy is the energy a body has because of its motion.
rubric.how: Award for identifying kinetic energy as energy possessed due to motion.

rubric.why: Uses work done to find the energy gained.
rubric.how: Award for relating kinetic energy gained to work done, W = Fs.

rubric.why: Uses Newton's second law and the motion relation for a body starting from rest.
rubric.how: Award for using F = ma and v² = 2as (or s = v²/2a).

rubric.why: Substitution gives the standard kinetic-energy equation.
rubric.how: Award for deriving or stating K.E. = ½mv².

modelAnswer: Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by a body due to its motion.
The kinetic energy gained by a body equals the work done on it: K.E. = W = Fs.
For a body of mass m starting from rest, F = ma and v² = 2as, so s = v²/(2a).
Therefore, K.E. = Fs = ma × v²/(2a) = ½mv².

items.followUp: What prefix represents 10⁻³? Give its symbol and an example.

rubric.why: Prefixes indicate decimal multiples or submultiples of units.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that prefixes are additions to unit names or symbols that show multiples or submultiples (powers of ten).

rubric.why: A correct example illustrates how a prefix is used.
rubric.how: Award for an example such as kilo = 1000, kilometre (km), or milli = 0.001.

modelAnswer: Prefixes are added to the names or symbols of units to show their decimal multiples or submultiples.
For example, kilo (k) means 1000, so 1 kilometre (km) = 1000 metres.

items.followUp: Name two methods used to increase friction.

rubric.why: Lubricants reduce direct contact between surfaces and reduce friction.
rubric.how: Award for naming lubrication or applying oil/grease between surfaces.

rubric.why: Rolling replaces sliding and reduces friction.
rubric.how: Award for naming ball bearings, rollers, or wheels; polishing surfaces or streamlining are also acceptable alternatives.

modelAnswer: Lubricate the surfaces with oil or grease.
Use ball bearings or rollers to replace sliding friction with rolling friction.

items.followUp: Give two examples of derived quantities and state the base quantities from which each is formed.

rubric.why: Base quantities are fundamental and are not defined in terms of other quantities.
rubric.how: Award for stating that base quantities are independent or fundamental quantities.

rubric.why: Derived quantities are obtained from combinations of base quantities.
rubric.description: Explains derived quantities and distinguishes them from base quantities.
rubric.how: Award for stating that derived quantities are formed from base quantities, for example speed = distance/time.

modelAnswer: Base quantities are independent fundamental quantities; they are not defined in terms of other quantities.
Derived quantities are obtained by combining base quantities, for example speed = distance/time.
